content.v: https://assets-prd.ignimgs.com/2026/08/11/tes6-1786479096622.jpg
A new report claims the next Elder Scrolls game will be titled The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel , along with new story details.

According to The Verge , The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel is the title of the highly-anticipated follow-up to Bethesda's Skyrim. This title has been rumored for some time now , but The Verge is putting extra weight behind it. According to the outlet, the game's title could be formally announced as soon as next month, possibly aligned with either Skyrim's 15th anniversary or Xbox's 25th anniversary. The game will reportedly take place in Hammerfell and dive into the history of the titular artifacts, allowing players to discover their secrets firsthand for the first time.

All of this is pretty exciting and shows that the game is likely getting closer to release. While we're not quite sure when to expect The Elder Scrolls 6, it wouldn't be surprising if we hear more details next year ahead of a 2028 release. However, Bethesda does like to wait until its games are close to the finish line to really lay it all out there, so we may be waiting a while before we get raw gameplay.

The road to The Elder Scrolls 6 has been quite long, as Bethesda announced the game back in 2018. At that stage, the game was still in the very, very early stages of pre-production. It may not have even really been anything more than a concept at that point, since Bethesda was full steam ahead on Starfield, which wouldn't release for another five years from that point. Since shipping Starfield, The Elder Scrolls 6 has become a massive priority and the studio's focus going forward.

Although there is a lot happening in and around Bethesda with future Fallout games, re-releases, and Starfield updates, The Elder Scrolls 6 seems to be taking the bulk of the developer's focus. The only question now is: will it all be worth the long wait?

items.title: 丹尼斯·戴克 (Denis Dyack) 表示，“AAA 出版商正在滥用抢先体验”，这让其他人的处境变得更加困难
items.summary: Dyack believes that games like Subnautica 2 are "skewing player expectations" for early access games.

content.v: Denis Dyack, known for his work on games including Blood Omen: Legacy of Kain and Eternal Darkness: Sanity's Requiem, says big game developers are "abusing early access" by using it as a marketing tool for highly polished games that are ready for full release anyway. That, Dyack believes, has shifted expectations for early access releases overall, and made life more difficult for indie developers who rely on the process to actually get their games finished and launched.

"They can put up a polished product and rake in cash," Dyack told GamesIndustry . "It's a marketing beat for them. So, that leaves players often expecting a near-perfect game that, in our opinion, defeats the purpose of early access, which is a collaborative development process based on player feedback.
"AAA publishers are abusing early access, skewing player expectations in such a way that it heavily disadvantages smaller independent developers."

Dyack said games like Subnautica 2 and Path of Exile are "drastically changing the landscape and players' expectations," which in turn has led to "significant barriers to entry" for less polished games like Dyack's current project, Deadhaus Sonata , which is now in early access on Steam.

Ethan McKinnon, who joined Deadhaus Sonata developer Apocalypse Studios as creative director after the game's rough early access launch earlier this year, added that "players naturally compare everything in the same marketplace, so smaller teams are being held to a much higher standard than they were in the past."

Interestingly, Subnautica 2 creative director Anthony Gallegos seemed to agree with at least part of Dyack's proposition, saying in the same report that early access is "not a few edge-case games participating anymore."

"Early access could mean a game like ours doing long-term open development, or it could be a game three months from a 1.0 release that's effectively doing a paid beta soft launch and using the Early Access term as a way to soften player expectations," Gallegos said. The result, he continued, is a "more diverse and confusing landscape."

I think that point is more salient here than any perceived 'abuse' by big publishers: It's tough to set meaningful broad expectations for "early access" when it's such a loosely defined term in the first place. But even though I'm not entirely convinced by Dyack's argument, he and McKinnon do have sensible advice for developers looking at early access launches: Ensure the game runs well, pay attention to Steam reviews, and connect with influencers who can get it in front of eyeballs.

Dyack admitted that Apocalypse Studios missed those points with the early access release of Deadhaus Sonata earlier this year. "We failed to prioritize the basics right from the get-go," Dyack said. "Also, we didn't handle Unreal Engine properly at the time and didn't do a good job explaining what made our game cool and different. In a lot of ways, we were too focused on what made our game so different and unique that it took our attention away from making sure we got the basics done right."
McKinnon put it more simply: "Developers need to treat early access like a real launch, because players do."

items.summary: Stephen Bliss, the former Rockstar Games artist who helped establish Grand Theft Auto's iconic visual style, h

content.v: https://assets-prd.ignimgs.com/2026/10/13/gta-3-cover-blog-1791888082659.jpg

Stephen Bliss, the former Rockstar Games artist who helped establish Grand Theft Auto's iconic visual style, has said he's flattered to see elements of his original designs continue to appear in the cover art for GTA 6.

Speaking to IGN at Lucca Comics and Games, Bliss, who worked at Rockstar from 2001 to 2016, reflected on his contribution to the series and how his work continues to influence its visual identity, even a decade after his departure.

"Well, I looked at the GTA 6 cover, for example. I had nothing to do with that, but the fact they still use the box grid and they still put the helicopter in the top left corner, which was something that I developed, I'm flattered by that," Bliss said. "It touches me that that heritage continues. And my influence is in the GTA 6 cover, but it's its own language. I just have little references in there. I'm like, 'Oh, that's nice that they used that.' But I'm absolutely not saying I contributed to that massively."

Bliss was instrumental in establishing the comic book-inspired look of Grand Theft Auto's promotional artwork, including the grid layout that has become synonymous with the franchise. However, he was also keen to emphasize the contributions of other Rockstar artists, including Anthony Macbain and Steven Olds.

Bliss explained that while he's spent the past decade establishing his own artistic identity outside Rockstar, he remains grateful for his time working on the series and the impact it continues to have.

The full interview with Bliss also explores how the September 11 attacks influenced the GTA 3 cover art, and the creative challenges behind the distinctive visual styles of Vice City and San Andreas. Check it out here .

items.summary: As a senior artist at Rockstar Games from 2001 to 2016, Stephen Bliss defined the iconic pop art and comic boo

content.v: https://assets-prd.ignimgs.com/2026/10/29/gtacovers-blogroll-1793289918640.jpeg

You might not immediately recognize the name Stephen Bliss, but I guarantee you'll recognize his work on arguably the most influential game franchise of our time. As a senior artist at Rockstar Games from 2001 to 2016, he defined the iconic pop art and comic book feel that has become the visual hallmark for Grand Theft Auto. IGN spoke to him at the Lucca Comics and Games festival about his work with the series, what he's been working on since, and finding the balance between making a name for himself away from the brand and seeing his artistic impact continue even as he works on other projects.

IGN: I was reading an interview with you where you said you didn't want to be known as the GTA guy, but you take it as an affirmation that people know your work and are inspired by that. Is that something that has been tricky to navigate in the past 10 years?

Stephen Bliss: I wanted to make a name for myself away from Rockstar in fine art and to make my own IPs, my own properties, and cartoons. And that's worked to a degree, and it's getting stronger all the time, my career. But I can't ignore what working at Rockstar has done for me. I'm very grateful for getting a job there and working there for such a long time. After GTA 3, Vice City, and Warriors, the team came in, Anthony Macbain [Director of Illustration at Rockstar for 13 years] and Steven Olds [former visualization director at Rockstar Games], who are both amazing artists. So when people tell me that they love my work, I might not completely be overwhelmed with the flattery of that, because other people did the work, and I don't want other people to think that I did all the work. When I said that quote before, what I meant was I don't want to take all the credit.

People have been bringing me GTA 5 covers to sign, and I say sorry, because I didn't work on that. And they look disappointed, but I've got to let people know what I did and what I didn't do. But I did contribute massively to Rockstar. And as I said, I'm grateful for that. And sometimes it can be like people are walking past my stand and they'll see all my personal work, Fear City work, and gig posters I did for bands and comics I've done, but they're really interested in more in the GTA getting that signed, or they're interested in a poster that's inspired by GTA for Lucca. But that's okay, because I did something well.
https://assets-prd.ignimgs.com/2026/09/29/9245b6dd45a143b26a7877ec5a29bb5c3fc00eda-1790721291674.webp
IGN: What you did, it set a standard; it set a style. I know there were other contributors to that, but as an artist, is that something that you see as an affirmation?

Stephen Bliss: Well, I looked at the GTA 6 cover, for example. I had nothing to do with that, but the fact they still use the box grid and they still put the helicopter in the top left corner, which was something that I developed, I'm flattered by that. It touches me that that heritage continues. And my influence is in the GTA 6 cover, but it's its own language. I just have little references in there. I'm like, 'Oh, that's nice that they used that.' But I'm absolutely not saying I contributed to that massively.

IGN: Is it difficult to convey something that is telling part of a story that sucks people in but isn't telling a whole story? Is that a challenge? Is that a puzzle that you have to solve as an artist?

Stephen Bliss: Yeah. What I'm missing with my work since I left Rockstar, for example, is that there's an emotional connection with people growing up and seeing that GTA work, which has actually been a good lesson for me recently. I realized that whatever I do from now on has to create an emotional connection. And even if I draw the anatomy badly or I'm being anal about getting everything correct, if it doesn't connect with someone emotionally, then that's where there's a disconnection. So I'm trying now to create some kind of emotional connection, which I'm not quite sure how I do that right now.
IGN: Is there a trick to that, or is it just kind of feeling your way through it?

Stephen Bliss: I know I've been trying to do it for 10 years since I left, and even Steroid [a t-shirt company Bliss set up with his brother], my project before I came to New York. I'm trying to revive that. And I've got the Fear City IP [a NFT series on the Ethereum blockchain], and I've got the Looby IP [an art-focused cryptocurrency], and my ambition now is to pull them all together as the Stephen Bliss brand. What I need is someone to finance that and market it. Those are the two major things that are missing. There have been people [who have come in with money], but they're full of shit really. But I'm hoping at some point someone will come in as a decent person and invest in it.

IGN: In an interview that Dan Hauser did with IGN , he mentioned you and the post-9/11 cover update. Is there anything that you remember about that process? Were they all-nighters where you just had to sit there and really lock in and change everything?

Stephen Bliss: Well, it was a lot to ask, to do a nonviolent GTA cover. But I understood because I personally was thinking, “Is entertainment from now on going to be all musicals and comedies and Disney? How are we going to be able to sell something that has a degree of violence in it?” And nobody knew. I was convinced it's all musicals [from- now on]. So when they asked for that, even though the [white] GTA 3 cover took me six months to paint, I'd always had in my head the grid system. “How can I chop these out? Chop out the nonviolent images, and what are you going to do with them?” I put them in a grid system because I grew up with Marvel and DC. I found a picture the other day - that really reminded me of that GTA cover - that I did when I was 10.

So for me it was almost... I mean, it was literally two nights. It wasn't an all-nighter, I don't think. Sometimes I'm pleased with myself; it's like I can get ideas really quickly. I may not be too bright on finance and investments, but I can come up with abstract ideas pretty quickly. And that was one of the big ones.
IGN: Were there any particular series or comics from Marvel or DC that really had a long-lasting impact or major impact with you, either on the GTA covers or your other work?

Stephen Bliss: Looking at the comic collection that I still have from when I was a kid, it was Spider-Man and the Titans. The Hulk and Spider-Man were the [ones] that I still have from when I was a kid. I still love Spider-Man and the Hulk. I still get excited about seeing them in the movies.

IGN: We were talking about Vice City and GTA San Andreas. There’s very obviously a Stephen Bliss style. I know you said other people contributed, but Vice City is obviously very colorful, and then you moved on to something a little bit grittier. Does that require a change in process? Or was it just like, “This is the brief, this is the game, this is how I'm going to take my style and bring it to life in a different environment?"

Stephen Bliss: Well, so after Vice City there was... I did Warriors on my own, and that was a real challenge, because I had to do a style that was completely different from GTA 3 but similar. And I started off doing it as GTA 3 because that's my style, that's my natural style. And then I just had to go completely out of the box and do that really kind of photographic painting. Somehow I had to find a way to do it. And that was always the case; find a way to do it. I still do that now with my freelance work. I say to my agent sometimes, I don't want to do it because I can't do it. And I do it because he always persuades me to do it. And I always feel pretty good about that, that I'm like, "Wow, I did something I didn't think I could do."

items.title: Xbox 希望到 2030 年比 PlayStation 和任天堂更有利可图
items.summary: Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has an ambitious goal: not only to make Xbox more lucrative, but to surpass the profit ma

content.v: Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has an ambitious goal: not only to make Xbox more lucrative, but to surpass the profit margins of its biggest gaming rivals, Sony and Nintendo.

Speaking to CNBC , Sharma said Microsoft was working to achieve this goal by mid-2030 and had a variety of plans in place, from focusing on more exclusive titles to gaining more ground in the casual games market. "We will build long-term plans for our biggest franchises across film, television, consumer products, sponsorship, live experiences, and form new partnerships globally, including China," Sharma wrote in an Xbox memo, adding that the company will invest heavily in Minecraft and that revenue growth is expected to speed up in the 2028 and 2029 fiscal years.
"By Financial Year 2030, our ambition is to be halfway to our long-term daily-player goal with sustained double-digit growth in players and engagement and industry-leading margins," she wrote.

While Sharma aims to increase Xbox's player and revenue growth in the fiscal year ending June 2027, things don't look too good for the division right now. According to Circana tracking data , US Xbox Series hardware sales fell 27% year-over-year in September 2026--reaching a new all-time September low--and Sharma recently posted online that revenue had declined in the most recent financial quarter. Sharma added that "console sales remain constrained by supply," but she was vague on the specifics. At the same time, Xbox console prices rose again in August, making it more expensive than ever to buy one compared with its original launch price in November 2020.

Xbox has also gone through a brutal "reset" phase ever since Sharma took over, with over 1,600 jobs eliminated and several studios cut from the Xbox portfolio. If Microsoft wants to make Xbox more profitable than Sony and Nintendo, it could face an uphill battle, as Xbox recorded a 10% quarterly revenue decline. By comparison, CNBC reported that Sony reached a 9.9% operating margin from game and network services alone in its latest financial year, while Nintendo was close to 16% in its fiscal year.

Xbox's current strategy seems focused on more than just gaming, as the new XP division was unveiled earlier this month. Dedicated to movies, TV, and live events, it follows several recent multimedia project announcements, including the third season of the Fallout TV series , a Call of Duty movie , a Diablo animated series , and a Minecraft theme park opening in 2027.

items.title: 专家称 Xbox 最近的努力没有改变任何事情，未来仍然黯淡
items.summary: Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has undertaken a number of efforts thus far to help get the business back into a healthy

content.v: Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has undertaken a number of efforts thus far to help get the business back into a healthy place, and nothing has worked, Circana analyst Mat Piscatella says.
He told The Game Business that based on the sales and engagement data he sees for the US gaming industry, "I'm not seeing [the moves] have any positive impact" for Xbox.

The disc-to-digital program "hasn't changed their sales of new physical software trend at all," he added. Additionally, making Gears of War: E-Day exclusive on console to Xbox "hasn't made any difference" in terms of selling more Xbox hardware. In fact, Xbox sales continue to spiral . Sharma says there is a supply issue, but, in the US at least, you can get a new Xbox very easily .

Piscatella said E-Day is a "Gears-ass Gears of War game," and a gorgeous one. But making it exclusive to Xbox created a scenario where "you chop the legs out" from under its potential potential to boost Xbox generally. "At least in the short term, it hasn't made a difference," he said.

There was clear and obvious evidence that E-Day was planned for PS5 , but it was never released on Sony's console. Other industry experts said Microsoft purposefully sent E-Day out to die "for hearts and minds."

Additionally, Piscatella said Sharma's decision to remove new Call of Duty games from Game Pass was another loser of a decision. He said the data he's seeing shows that the Call of Duty franchise "lost a ton of engagement" due to Modern Warfare 4 being stripped out of Game Pass.
"And you got no benefit. It’s really hard to find any signs of positivity or hope on that platform right now," he said.

Piscatella went on to say that the efforts Microsoft is undertaking are for "Twitter likes" from hardcore fans. "But other than that, in terms of actual results, I'm not seeing anything right now," he said.

Sharma's turnaround plan for Xbox was never expected to yield immediate results--she only took the job in February and she inherited numerous foundational problems. In a memo to staff seen by CNBC , Sharma said she's taking a "long-term" view to help turn things around, and that includes pushing every studio to return to growth for players and revenue by the end of the fiscal year ending June 2027. Beyond games, Sharma has established a unit called XP , which will expand Xbox's games across film, TV, consumer products, sponsorships, and live experiences, as well as new initiatives in China.

Also in the memo, Sharma said she will push her teams to help Xbox get back in line with rivals Sony and Nintendo by 2027 in terms of profit margins, and then beat them by mid-2030. For comparison, Xbox currently reports about a 3% internal margin, which compares to 9.9% for PlayStation and 16% for Nintendo, according to CNBC.
A 3% profit margin means that for every $100 that Xbox brings in, it spent $97 to do so and keeps $3. A higher profit margin is better, and that's what Sharma is pushing for.
